Introduction & Executive Summary** #### **1.1 Introduction** In this Quarterly report, we have amended our supplydemand balance and price projections out to 2011. We assess the market under three separate scenarios. This is particularly relevant at this stage of the economic cycle given the massive uncertainty associated with the credit crunch. Reflecting this, we ascribe similar probabilities (40%) to our Base case as to our two alternative scenarios (30% each) which we describe as scenario B and C. of $2,812/tonne. As we have discussed in our previous research, the main theme in the copper market has been the battle between tight supply and the increasingly weak demand environment. Although the former remains a feature of the market, with examples being the grade problems keeping Chilean output low and African Copperbelt production once again failing to live up to potential, the latter has become increasingly dominant. #### **1.2 Assumptions/terminology** GFMS Metals Consulting analyses the copper balance on a global basis. However in our analysis of demand, we draw a distinction between the mature economies (Japan, US and Europe) and the emerging economies. Within this latter category, we look in detail at trends within the BRICs (Brazil, Russia, India and China) and a grouping we refer to as SEATAK - South-east Asia (the ASEAN economies) and South Korea and Taiwan. #### **1.3 Background** Although copper prices were among the last of the base metals to peak at $8,985/tonne on July 3 2008, the performance since then has been remarkably similar to the rest of the sector. Copper prices have given up the bulk of their gains, falling by 69% to a recent low The bottom line, ofcourse, has been that inventories have risen sharply. Not surprisingly the bulk of the increase has taken place on the LME, the market of “last resort”. Figures 1.1 and 1.2 highlight trends in both LME and total reported stocks versus the price. The most closely watched indicator, LME stocks, now stands at 2.1 weeks’ consumption compared to the cycle low of just one day. However current inventories are still comfortably below the levels seen prior to the b

ull market for example in 2003 when they represented over 4 weeks’ consumption. In Figure 1.3, we highlight the position of copper compared to the other metals. This massive federal spending and tax cut programme will be financed by issuing additional federal debt, with the potential for the Federal Reserve to begin buying some of these securities directly from the Treasury. We also believe the Federal Reserve will keep interest rates low for an extended period of time in order to support economic recovery and avoid jeopardising a convalescing economy. As such, US GDP, after contracting by 0.5% in 2009, resumes its growth by posting an increase of 3.0% and 3.5% in 2010 and 2011 respectively. Taking into account the fact that the US economy escapes a prolonged recession, and its consumer spending starts to recover, the global economy also improves, partly due to an increase in US imports. Global GDP growth under this scenario shrinks to 1.7% in 2009 and then expands by 3.4% and 3.8% in 2010 and 2011 respectively. **Scenario C:** (weighted with a 30% probability outcome). The global economy is expected to shrink by 0.1% in 2009 and then remain under pressure, posting growth of only 1.5% and 2.5% in 2010 and 2011 respectively. This is based on our expectations for GDP growth

In Figure 1.6, we highlight the quarterly year-on-year change in copper consumption during the bull market. The rate of growth peaked in Q1 2007 and was just 0.5% in Q4 2008 and we believe that it will again turn negative in Q1 2009. #### **1.9 Production Costs** 

In mid 2008, the focus of the market was still on the increase in production costs and the conventional wisdom at the time was that there had been a structural shift in the cost curve.  This reflected problems with lower grades, new projects having to be developed in increasingly inaccessible places and higher equipment, energy, labour and other input costs. Although some of these issues are still relevant, many of the cost increases proved merely to be cyclical rather than structural.  Lead times for mining equipment have been slashed, while the skill shortage seems to have disappeared overnight, with the large scale lay-off of mining staff, and energy, sulphuric acid and other input prices have collapsed.

#### **1.10 Industry Consolidation** 

Industry consolidation has been put on hold by the collapse in prices and by the credit crunch.  However GFMS Metals Consulting has always thought that the impact of greater industry consolidation on price levels was always overstated.  We note that the greater amount of consolidation in the nickel industry has not lead to a superior performance for that metal in this down cycle, or for that matter in previous down cycles. 

GFMS Metals Consulting estimates the marginal cost of production (based on the ninth decile) to be around $3,300/tonne similar to the level prevailing in mid February.   The price of most of the other base metals currently resides in between the fifth and the seventh decile.   If the copper market follows the other metals down the cost curve (and we do not see any particular reason for this not to be the case), then there is further downside potential in the copper market. Given developments in Q4, it would be surprising if unreported stocks had not been built up. ##### **Demand projections scaled back** The single biggest change to our analysis is that we now believe that global consumption will decline this year by 0.2% compared to an earlier projection of 3.7% growth. We would view our projection as fairly conservative i.e. positive given direction in which nearly all of the demand indicators are pointing. Once again, the copper industry will be heavily reliant on China to support demand growth, as we have demand in the mature economies falling by 3.7% this year. We have assumed quite a sharp rebound in 2010. One positive factor on the demand side is that pipeline stocks in the consumption/distribution chain are low. Therefore, if economic activity does improve, even relatively modestly, this would trigger a restocking process that should support 4.5% growth in demand in 2010. In 2011, we expect an acceleration of economic growth. The focus of the market may switch back to the prospects for strong growth from the emerging economies. In addition, the benefits of industrialisation and urbanisation to copper demand may once again be mentioned. We are also looking for a sharp recovery in prices, whi

ch in itself will trigger off another bout of restocking, that should result in a year of significantly above trend demand growth (+ 6.3%). ##### **Double guessing the producers** In this report, we have taken into consideration cutbacks that have taken place so far. The duration of the cuts is by no means clear. We have assumed that most cutbacks remain in place in 2009 and are gradually phased back in during 2010. In our base case, we have assumed no further major cutbacks on price grounds. We cover that (likely) prospect in our alternative scenarios. One reason for this is that copper prices still reside in the steep tail of the cost curve, where a decline in prices does not automatically lead to an immediate or large cut back in output. There is plenty of scope for cutbacks arising from the usual problems of strikes, technical problems, lower grades and the on-going uncertainty concerning output in the African Copperbelt. We have taken account of these potential losses in our projections. ##### **Double guessing the State Reserves Bureau (SRB)** Rumours concerning the level of SRB purchases have supported the copper price in early February with reports suggesting purchases of between 100,000 to 1m tonnes. We are assuming only limited purchases by the SRB and that these will be overshadowed by weak global demand. We caution against letting such an uncertain component of the market alter our base case scenario for the red metal. Prices in early February have traded a $3,071-3,527/ tonne range. Our average forecast of $3,000/tonne implies that prices will fall but not collapse from current levels. We expect that bottom of the market (taking into consideration the potential for a short-lived overshoot) will be $2,600/tonne. Upside moves should be capped at $3,500/tonne.
